sources.title: WebP Container Specification
supports: A WebP file is a RIFF container whose first chunk is 'VP8 ' (lossy), 'VP8L' (lossless), or 'VP8X' (extended)
sources.note: The byte offsets used in src/inspect.ts were checked against files written by cwebp, not derived from this page alone.

sources.title: Graphics Interchange Format, Version 89a
supports: A GIF data stream starts with a 3-byte signature and a 3-byte version, followed by the logical screen width and height as unsigned 16-bit values

sources.title: Cloudflare Queues: Delivery guarantees
supports: Queues provides at-least-once delivery by default; a message may on rare occasions be delivered more than once
Cloudflare suggests a unique ID used as a primary key or an idempotency key to de-duplicate

sources.title: Cloudflare Queues: Batching, Retries and Delays
supports: A consumer receives batches; max_batch_size defaults to 10 and max_batch_timeout to 5 seconds
ack() and retry() on a single message acknowledge or redeliver just that message
max_retries defaults to 3; after that a message is deleted, or written to the dead-letter queue if one is configured

sources.title: Cloudflare Queues: Dead Letter Queues
supports: A dead-letter queue is set in the consumer configuration and is a queue like any other
Without one, messages that reach the retry limit are deleted permanently

sources.title: Cloudflare R2: Event notifications
supports: R2 sends object-create and object-delete notifications to a Cloudflare Queue, with optional prefix and suffix rules
The example message has account, bucket, object key, size and eTag, action, and eventTime
sources.note: No field corresponding to S3's sequencer appears in the message format on this page.

sources.title: Cloudflare Workers: Cron Triggers
supports: A Worker can be run on a schedule with a cron expression through its scheduled() handler
sources.note: The page was not found to state a delivery guarantee for scheduled runs.

sources.title: Improve the security of EC2 instances by using VPC endpoints for Systems Manager
supports: The page lists the interface endpoints ssm, ec2messages, and ssmmessages, plus S3 for SSM Agent updates
ssmmessages is required for SSM Agent to communicate with Systems Manager, for Run Command, and for Session Manager
Beginning with SSM Agent 3.3.40.0, Systems Manager uses the ssmmessages endpoint whenever available instead of ec2messages
Without endpoints, the instance needs outbound HTTPS (443) to the ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages endpoints
SSM Agent initiates all connections, so no inbound traffic has to be allowed
The security group of an endpoint must allow inbound 443 from the instance's subnet
A logs endpoint is needed to send Session Manager, Run Command, or agent logs to CloudWatch Logs without internet access

sources.title: Reference: ec2messages, ssmmessages, and other API operations
supports: With SSM Agent 3.3.40.0 or later and ssmmessages permissions, the agent connects to ssmmessages even when both are allowed
In Regions launched before 2024, ec2messages permissions can be removed from policies; Regions launched in 2024 and later support only ssmmessages
sources.note: The page speaks of IAM permissions. It does not say in so many words that the ec2messages VPC endpoint can be left out, so this chapter keeps all three endpoints.

sources.title: Find AMIs with the SSM Agent preinstalled
supports: SSM Agent is preinstalled on Amazon Linux 2023 AMIs provided by AWS
The preinstalled version might not be the latest

sources.title: SSM Agent technical reference
supports: SSM Agent creates the local ssm-user account and adds it to /etc/sudoers.d; it is the default OS user of a session
The agent must reach AWS managed S3 buckets such as aws-ssm-<region> and patch-baseline-snapshot-<region>

sources.title: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
supports: Session Manager needs no open inbound ports, no bastion hosts, and no SSH keys
Access is controlled with IAM policies; port forwarding redirects a port on the managed node to a local port
Session activity can be logged through CloudTrail, S3, and CloudWatch Logs

sources.title: Step 1: Complete Session Manager prerequisites
supports: Port forwarding needs SSM Agent 3.0.222.0 or later on the managed node
Sessions run as ssm-user, an account with root or administrator permissions that the agent creates

sources.title: Start a session
supports: aws ssm start-session --target <instance id> starts a session and needs the Session Manager plugin on the local machine
AWS-StartPortForwardingSession takes portNumber and localPortNumber parameters

sources.title: Install the Session Manager plugin for the AWS CLI
supports: The Session Manager plugin must be installed separately on the local machine to start sessions with the AWS CLI
The page asks for plugin version 1.2.764.0 or later

sources.title: Configure instance permissions required for Systems Manager
supports: An instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore is one of the two documented ways to let Systems Manager manage an instance
The other is Default Host Management Configuration at the account level, which this chapter does not use

sources.title: AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore (AWS managed policy reference)
supports: The policy (version v2) allows ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages actions on Resource "*"
Among them are ssm:GetParameter and ssm:GetParameters on every resource

sources.title: Walkthrough: Use the AWS CLI with Run Command
supports: AWS-RunShellScript runs commands on a managed node as if logged on locally
Commands in the pre-configured AWS-* documents run with administrative permissions; a user allowed to run them has administrator access to the node
send-command returns a command ID; get-command-invocation returns the result per instance

sources.title: GetCommandInvocation (Systems Manager API reference)
supports: Status is one of Pending, InProgress, Delayed, Success, Cancelled, TimedOut, Failed, Cancelling
ResponseCode is the script's exit code; StandardOutputContent holds the first 24,000 characters of stdout

sources.title: AWS Systems Manager pricing
supports: Session Manager, Run Command, and Patch Manager have no additional charge for use on Amazon EC2 instances
From September 30, 2026, sessions and Run Command invocations on hybrid and multicloud nodes are billed

sources.title: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager
supports: Patch Manager can scan managed nodes for missing patches or scan and install them, and reports compliance

sources.title: Patch Manager prerequisites
supports: Without internet access, nodes must still reach their configured patch repositories and the AWS managed S3 buckets

sources.title: How patch baseline rules work on Linux-based systems
supports: On AL2023 EC2 instances, Patch Manager uses the latest repository versions, independent of the version the system is locked to

sources.title: Use the Instance Metadata Service to access instance metadata
supports: IMDS answers at 169.254.169.254; IMDSv2 is session-oriented: a PUT request returns a token that later requests must present
PUT requests carrying an X-Forwarded-For header are rejected
The response to the PUT has a hop limit of 1 by default

sources.title: Configure the Instance Metadata Service options
supports: The hop limit can be 1 to 64; a hop limit of 1 can cause issues in a container environment
Options not given at launch come from account-level defaults, then from the AMI

sources.title: IMDSv2 (Amazon Linux 2023 User Guide)
supports: Instances launched from the AL2023 AMI require IMDSv2 and get a hop limit of 2 by default

sources.title: IAM roles for Amazon EC2
supports: Applications on an instance retrieve temporary credentials for the instance's role from instance metadata
An instance profile can contain only one IAM role

sources.title: Run commands when you launch an EC2 instance with user data input
supports: User data scripts run only during the boot cycle of the first launch, by default
They run as root, not interactively; output goes to /var/log/cloud-init-output.log
User data is limited to 16 KB before base64 encoding

sources.title: Amazon EC2 instance state changes
supports: A stopped instance is not billed for instance usage, but its EBS volumes are still charged
A running instance is billed per second with a one-minute minimum, even when idle
EBS volumes and Elastic IP addresses incur charges regardless of the instance's state

sources.title: Stop and start Amazon EC2 instances
supports: A started instance typically moves to a new host and gets a new public IPv4 address
Data on instance store volumes is erased when an instance stops

sources.title: Amazon EC2 instance IP addressing
supports: An auto-assigned public IPv4 address is released when the instance is stopped, hibernated, or terminated, and a new one is assigned on start
A persistent public address needs an Elastic IP address

sources.title: Automatic instance recovery
supports: Simplified automatic recovery is enabled by default on supported instances and acts when a system status check fails
A recovered instance keeps its instance ID, IP addresses, attached EBS volumes, and Availability Zone, and loses what was in memory
Automatic recovery does not operate when only the instance status check fails

sources.title: Configure simplified automatic recovery on an Amazon EC2 instance
supports: Simplified automatic recovery needs available capacity and does not operate during service events in the AWS Health Dashboard
It is not supported for instances with instance store volumes, metal sizes, or Dedicated Hosts

sources.title: Status checks for Amazon EC2 instances
supports: System status checks detect problems with the AWS systems under the instance; instance status checks detect problems you must fix yourself
Status checks run every minute

sources.title: Unlimited mode concepts for burstable performance instances
supports: T4g, T3a, T3, and T8i instances launch in unlimited mode by default
In unlimited mode, CPU use above the baseline averaged over 24 hours is billed at a flat rate per vCPU-hour

sources.title: Preserve data when an instance is terminated
supports: By default the root volume is deleted on termination, and a data volume attached after launch is preserved
The default at launch comes from the DeleteOnTermination attribute in the AMI

sources.title: AL2023 on Amazon EC2
supports: The latest AL2023 AMI is published under /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/, for example al2023-ami-kernel-default-arm64
From August 17, 2026 the default kernel of al2023-ami-kernel-default AMIs is 6.18; version-specific AMIs such as kernel-6.1 remain

sources.title: Deterministic upgrades through versioned repositories on AL2023
supports: An AL2023 instance is locked to the repository version its AMI was built from and does not receive newer updates on its own
dnf check-release-update lists newer releases; dnf upgrade --releasever=<version> moves to one
The AMI behind the SSM parameter is always the latest version

sources.title: Updating AL2023
supports: Running dnf with --releasever=latest is called out as not best practice; a specific release version should be named

sources.title: Deterministic updates via instance replacement
supports: Replacing instances with ones launched from a newer AMI is presented as a predictable way to roll out OS updates

sources.title: Node.js in AL2023
supports: AL2023 provides Node.js 20, 22, and 24 as namespaced packages (nodejs24) with versioned executables (node-24)
The plain `node` name is an alternatives link that can point at a different version

sources.title: AWS CLI v2 (Amazon Linux 2023 User Guide)
supports: AL2023 ships with AWS CLI version 2

sources.title: systemd journal replaces rsyslog
supports: AL2023 does not install rsyslog by default; logs are in the systemd journal and read with journalctl

sources.title: gp3 as default Amazon EBS volume type
supports: AL2023 AMIs use gp3 volumes by default, and XFS on the root file system

sources.title: Manage package and operating system updates in AL2023
supports: Sample dnf output shows the repositories at https://al2023-repos-<region>-de612dc2.s3.dualstack.<region>.amazonaws.com/
sources.note: This is the only evidence found that the repositories are S3 buckets in the instance's Region. No page read states that an S3 gateway endpoint is enough to reach them.

sources.title: Amazon EBS volumes
supports: An EBS volume persists independently of the life of an instance
The volume and the instance must be in the same Availability Zone

sources.title: Map Amazon EBS volumes to NVMe device names
supports: NVMe device names can change between boots; stable identifiers are recommended
Amazon Linux AMIs later than 2017.09.01 ship a udev rule that links the block device mapping name to the NVMe device

sources.title: Make an Amazon EBS volume available for use
supports: A new volume has no file system; mkfs on a volume that has data destroys it
fstab entries should use the UUID, with the nofail option so the instance boots without the volume

sources.title: Amazon EBS snapshots
supports: Snapshots are incremental, stored in Amazon S3, and replicated across the Availability Zones of the Region
A volume can be restored from a snapshot in any Availability Zone of that Region

sources.title: Create Amazon EBS snapshots
supports: Snapshot creation is asynchronous; the snapshot stays pending until its data has been transferred
For a consistent snapshot, pause writes or unmount the volume first; writes can resume once the snapshot is pending
Snapshots of encrypted volumes are encrypted

sources.title: Replace an Amazon EBS volume using a snapshot
supports: A volume created from a snapshot must be in the same Availability Zone as the instance it will attach to
aws ec2 create-volume takes --snapshot-id and --availability-zone

sources.title: Initialize Amazon EBS volumes
supports: Blocks of a volume created from a snapshot are downloaded from S3 on first access, which adds latency until the volume is initialized

sources.title: AWS::EC2::Instance
supports: ImageId: update requires replacement
UserData: update requires some interruptions; with an EBS root volume CloudFormation restarts the instance
CreditSpecification accepts standard and unlimited

sources.title: AWS::EC2::Volume
supports: A deletion policy can retain the volume, delete it, or create a snapshot before deleting it
AvailabilityZone and SnapshotId cannot be updated

sources.title: AWS::EC2::VolumeAttachment
supports: The volume must be unmounted inside the instance before the attachment is deleted, or it can be stuck in the busy state
Every property requires replacement on update

sources.title: AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile
supports: Only one role can be assigned to an EC2 instance at a time, and all applications on the instance share it

supports: A parameter of type AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id> makes CloudFormation fetch the value from Parameter Store when the stack is created or updated

sources.title: DeletionPolicy attribute
supports: Snapshot is supported for resources such as AWS::EC2::Volume; Retain is supported for any resource

sources.title: systemd v252: systemd.service(5)
supports: Restart=on-failure restarts on a non-zero exit code, a signal, a timeout, or a watchdog, not on a clean exit
TimeoutStopSec= is how long to wait for a stop before the service is terminated with SIGKILL
sources.note: The systemd version on Amazon Linux 2023 was not checked on an instance.

sources.title: systemd v252: systemd.unit(5)
supports: RequiresMountsFor= adds Requires= and After= on the mount units for a path
AssertPathIsMountPoint= fails the start when the path is not a mount point; ConditionPathExists= skips it quietly
StartLimitIntervalSec= and StartLimitBurst= limit how often a unit may be started

sources.title: systemd v252: systemd.exec(5)
supports: ProtectSystem=strict mounts the file system hierarchy read-only for the service; ReadWritePaths= makes exceptions
NoNewPrivileges=, ProtectHome=, PrivateTmp=, User=, and EnvironmentFile= behave as the unit in this chapter assumes

sources.title: systemd v252: systemd.kill(5)
supports: KillSignal= is the first signal sent on stop (SIGTERM by default), followed by SIGKILL after the timeout

sources.title: Node.js v24: HTTP, server.close()
supports: server.close() stops the server from accepting new connections and closes connections that are not sending a request or waiting for a response
server.closeAllConnections() closes every connection, including active ones

sources.title: Control traffic to your AWS resources using security groups
supports: Security groups do not filter traffic to Amazon DNS, DHCP, EC2 instance metadata, or the Amazon Time Sync Service

sources.title: Lambda quotas
supports: A function invocation can run for up to 900 seconds (15 minutes); memory is up to 10,240 MB

sources.title: Fargate task ephemeral storage for Amazon ECS
supports: A Fargate task on platform version 1.4.0 or later gets 20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default, up to 200 GiB

sources.title: AWS Fargate for Amazon ECS
supports: Fargate runs containers without servers or clusters of EC2 instances to manage
Each Fargate task has its own isolation boundary and does not share a kernel with another task; kernel and runtime updates arrive as platform version revisions

sources.title: Amazon ECS services
supports: When a task of a service fails or stops, the service scheduler launches another to replace it

sources.title: Configure ephemeral storage for Lambda functions
supports: Lambda gives each execution environment temporary storage in /tmp, configurable from 512 MB to 10,240 MB

sources.title: Health checks for instances in an Auto Scaling group
supports: An Auto Scaling group replaces an instance it finds unhealthy with a new one launched from its launch template

sources.title: Manually create or edit the CloudWatch agent configuration file
supports: The agent's logs section can collect systemd journal entries on Linux through a journald section

sources.title: Lambda durable functions
supports: A durable execution can run for up to one year; it uses checkpoints and recovers through replay, re-executing from the beginning while skipping completed work
Waits suspend execution without compute charges

The page's own comparison: durable functions run within Lambda in standard programming languages; Step Functions is a standalone service with a graph-based DSL and native integrations to 220+ services
The SDK is available for JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, and Java

sources.title: Lambda durable functions: Basic concepts
supports: On resume Lambda invokes the function again from the beginning and substitutes stored values for completed operations
Code must be deterministic during replay; random numbers and the current time belong inside steps
DurableConfig has ExecutionTimeout (default 86,400 s, 60 s to 31,536,000 s) and RetentionPeriodInDays (default 14, 1 to 90)
The Lambda function timeout (at most 15 minutes) limits each invocation; the execution timeout limits the whole durable execution

sources.title: Lambda durable functions: Idempotency
supports: Steps have at-least-once execution semantics by default; a step that fails or is interrupted before completing might execute multiple times
An execution name acts as an idempotency key: the same name with the same payload returns the existing execution, a different payload returns DurableExecutionAlreadyStartedException
Event source mappings do not support execution-name idempotency at launch

sources.title: Invoking durable Lambda functions
supports: A durable function must be invoked with a qualified identifier: a version number, an alias, or $LATEST
An execution is pinned to the function version that started it; $LATEST executions can resume on updated code
Synchronous invocations are limited to 15 minutes; asynchronous invocations support executions up to one year
Durable functions support dead-letter queues but not Lambda destinations

sources.title: Security and permissions for Lambda durable functions
supports: The execution role needs lambda:CheckpointDurableExecution and lambda:GetDurableExecutionState
Lambda authorizes most durable execution actions against the durable execution ARN, which extends a qualified function ARN; a policy naming the unqualified function ARN does not match
The managed policy AWSLambdaBasicDurableExecutionRolePolicy contains these permissions together with basic logging

sources.title: Deploy Lambda durable functions with Infrastructure as Code
supports: CloudFormation: AWS::Lambda::Function takes DurableConfig with ExecutionTimeout and RetentionPeriodInDays
The CDK example sets durableConfig on lambda.Function and invokes through an alias of currentVersion
IaC deployments must enable durable execution, grant checkpoint permissions, and publish a version or alias

sources.title: Supported runtimes for durable functions
supports: Managed runtimes that support durable functions include nodejs22.x and nodejs24.x
The Node.js runtimes include the SDK, and the page recommends bundling it in the deployment package anyway
The JavaScript SDK is the npm package @aws/durable-execution-sdk-js

sources.title: Durable execution SDK: how durable operations are metered
supports: Starting an execution counts as one operation; a step counts as one plus one per retry; a wait counts as one
Data persisted is the input payload and the payload returned by each step attempt

sources.title: Durable functions or Step Functions
supports: AWS's own guidance: durable functions when the logic lives mostly in Lambda and the team prefers code; Step Functions for orchestration across many AWS services, visual workflows, and zero-maintenance infrastructure

sources.title: Best practices for Lambda durable functions
supports: Do not rename steps or change their behavior while executions are in progress: replay matches saved state to step definitions
Unlike standard functions, Lambda does not automatically retry a failed durable execution after an asynchronous invocation; configure a dead-letter queue

sources.title: Lambda quotas (function timeout and durable functions)
supports: Function timeout: 900 seconds (15 minutes); the function configuration quotas cannot be changed except as noted, and the one noted exception is 5,400 seconds for Lambda Managed Instances
At most 3,000 durable operations per durable execution; cannot be increased
At most 100 MB of durable execution storage written per execution; cannot be increased
Durable function quotas apply per Region, with higher defaults in three named Regions
sources.note: The page lists no Regions where durable functions are unavailable. Availability in ap-northeast-1 was inferred only from the Price List entries (source aws-price-list-lambda-durable), not confirmed by running anything.

sources.title: Using the Lambda context object to retrieve Node.js function information
supports: context.getRemainingTimeInMillis() returns the milliseconds left before the execution times out

sources.title: AWS Durable Execution SDK Developer Guide: Key concepts
supports: For each durable operation the SDK checks for an existing checkpoint, runs the operation if there is none, serializes the result, and persists the checkpoint before continuing
The orchestration code must make the same sequence of durable operation calls on every invocation
After a wait, the SDK terminates the current Lambda invocation and the service invokes the function again later

sources.title: AWS Durable Execution SDK Developer Guide: Idempotency and retries
supports: At-least-once per retry is the default: if an attempt is interrupted (the sandbox dies, the network drops, the runtime hits the invocation timeout), the step runs again on replay
At-most-once per retry waits for the START checkpoint and raises StepInterrupted on replay instead of re-executing; neither semantic guarantees exactly one run across the workflow

sources.title: @aws/durable-execution-sdk-js 2.6.0 and @aws/durable-execution-sdk-js-testing 1.3.0 (npm tarballs)
supports: withDurableExecution wraps a handler that receives (event, DurableContext); context.step(name, fn, config) returns the checkpointed result
StepConfig accepts retryStrategy(error, attempt) returning { shouldRetry, delay } and semantics (StepSemantics.AtLeastOncePerRetry by default)
The testing package's LocalDurableTestRunner runs a handler against a checkpoint store in the local process, with skipTime to skip waits and retry delays
Both packages require Node.js 22 or later and depend on @aws-sdk/client-lambda
sources.note: Read from the installed tarballs (README and dist-types). Version 2.6.0 was published on 2026-10-02.

sources.title: Choosing workflow type in Step Functions
supports: Standard workflows run up to one year and are billed by state transition; Express workflows run up to five minutes and are billed by executions, duration, and memory
Standard workflows follow an exactly-once model: tasks and states are never run more than once unless Retry is specified in the definition
Asynchronous Express workflows are at-least-once
The workflow type cannot be changed after the state machine is created
Standard: starting an execution with the same name as a running one returns an idempotent response; execution history is removed after 90 days
Express workflows do not support the .sync or .waitForTaskToken integration patterns

sources.title: Handling errors in Step Functions workflows
supports: Retry fields: ErrorEquals, IntervalSeconds (default 1), MaxAttempts (default 3; 0 means never retried), BackoffRate (default 2.0), MaxDelaySeconds, JitterStrategy (FULL or NONE)
States.ALL matches any known error name but not States.DataLimitExceeded or States.Runtime; States.TaskFailed matches any error except States.Timeout
Catch has ErrorEquals, Next, and ResultPath; catchers apply when there is no Retry or retries are exhausted
Catchers exist for Task, Parallel, and Map states, not for top-level execution failures
Retries are treated as state transitions
Without Retry or Catch, an error fails the entire execution

sources.title: Task workflow state
supports: TimeoutSeconds: the maximum time a task can run before it fails with States.Timeout; the default is 99,999,999
The timeout counts from the task's start event; if the worker does not respond in time, Step Functions marks the task as failed
sources.note: The page says what Step Functions does when the time runs out. It does not say that the Lambda function is stopped.

sources.title: Invoke an AWS Lambda function with Step Functions
supports: A function ARN can be given directly in Resource; the task result is then the function's output alone, and .waitForTaskToken is not available
With the optimized integration (arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke) the function output is nested under Payload

sources.title: Handling error conditions in a Step Functions state machine
supports: An error thrown by a Node.js Lambda function is matched in Retry and Catch by the error's name (the tutorial sets this.name = 'CustomError' and catches "CustomError")
The tutorial retries Lambda.ServiceException, Lambda.AWSLambdaException, Lambda.SdkClientException, and Lambda.TooManyRequestsException

sources.title: Specifying state output using ResultPath in Step Functions
supports: ResultPath in a Catch keeps the state's input and adds the error under the given field

sources.title: Restarting state machine executions with redrive in Step Functions
supports: A failed, aborted, or timed-out Standard execution can be redriven for 14 days; it continues from the unsuccessful step with the same input and the same definition
Successful steps are not rerun; a redriven Task state is scheduled and started again with its retry count reset
A redrive re-enters a Fail state and fails again
Redrives count as state transitions; an execution with 24,999 or more history events cannot be redriven

sources.title: Step Functions service quotas
supports: Standard workflows: at most 25,000 events in one execution history; reaching it fails the execution
Input or output of a task, state, or execution is at most 256 KiB as a UTF-8 string
Execution history is kept for 90 days after an execution closes

sources.title: Best practices for Step Functions
supports: Without TimeoutSeconds on a Task, an execution can be stuck waiting for a response that never comes
To stay under the history quota, use a Distributed Map or start a new execution from a Task state

sources.title: Creating an IAM role for your state machine in Step Functions
supports: The state machine's role is assumed by states.amazonaws.com
The documented trust policy limits it with ArnLike aws:SourceArn arn:aws:states:<region>:<account>:stateMachine:* and StringEquals aws:SourceAccount

sources.title: Run Amazon ECS or Fargate tasks with Step Functions
supports: The optimized integration calls ecs:runTask and supports the Run a Job (.sync) pattern
With .sync, a non-empty Failures field fails the task with AmazonECS.Unknown
Input reaches the container through overrides (ContainerOverride)

sources.title: Discover service integration patterns in Step Functions
supports: With .sync Step Functions waits for the job to complete before moving on; AWS Batch submitJob.sync and ECS runTask.sync are examples
If a .sync task is aborted and Step Functions cannot cancel the job, the integrated service may keep charging

sources.title: StartExecution
supports: StartExecution is idempotent for STANDARD workflows: the same name and input as a running execution returns the same response
If the execution is closed or the input differs, it returns 400 ExecutionAlreadyExists; a name can be reused 90 days after the execution closes
An execution name is at most 80 characters and must not contain, among others, colons, slashes, brackets, or white space; without a name Step Functions generates a UUID

sources.title: AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine
supports: Properties include DefinitionString, RoleArn, StateMachineType, LoggingConfiguration, and DefinitionSubstitutions

sources.title: AWS Step Functions pricing
supports: Standard workflows are charged per state transition, retries included
The free tier is 4,000 state transitions a month, does not expire, and applies to existing and new customers
The page's example counts four transitions for a workflow of two states: Start, the two states, and End
sources.note: Prices on the page are filled in by script; the numbers used in the book come from the Price List (source aws-price-list-states).

sources.title: AWS Lambda pricing: Lambda Durable Functions Pricing
supports: Durable functions are charged for durable operations (starting executions, completing steps, creating waits), for data written, and for data retained during and after execution, on top of normal Lambda compute
During a wait an on-demand function incurs no duration charge until execution resumes
Compute charges apply to the invocations that replays cause
sources.note: The section names no free allowance for durable operations or storage.

sources.title: Adding context attributes in EventBridge Scheduler
supports: <aws.scheduler.scheduled-time> in the target's payload is replaced with the time the schedule was due, for example 2022-03-22T18:59:43Z
<aws.scheduler.execution-id> is unique per attempted invocation, and <aws.scheduler.attempt-number> counts attempts

sources.title: Using templated targets in EventBridge Scheduler: Step Functions StartExecution
supports: Step Functions StartExecution is a templated target: the target ARN is the state machine's, and Input is the execution input
The schedule's execution role needs states:StartExecution
sources.note: The page's example policy uses Resource "*"; the chapter's role names the one state machine instead.

sources.title: How to prevent object overwrites with conditional writes (re-read for chapter 16)
supports: PutObject with If-None-Match: * succeeds only if no object has the key; otherwise S3 answers 412 Precondition Failed
When several conditional writes target the same key, the first to finish succeeds and the rest get 412
A 409 Conflict is possible when a delete of the key succeeds before the conditional write completes; a PutObject may be retried after it
If-None-Match needs only the s3:PutObject permission

sources.title: Scanning tables in DynamoDB
supports: One Scan request reads at most 1 MB; the limit and the Limit parameter apply before the filter expression
The absence of LastEvaluatedKey is the only way to know the last page was reached; it is passed back as ExclusiveStartKey
Read capacity is consumed by the items read, whether or not a filter or projection drops them

sources.title: HeadObject (permissions, re-read for chapter 16)
supports: HEAD needs the s3:GetObject permission
For a missing object S3 answers 404 if the caller has s3:ListBucket on the bucket and 403 if not

sources.title: DynamoDB data export to Amazon S3: how it works
supports: Export to S3 exports a table as of any time within its point-in-time recovery window; PITR must be enabled on the table
sources.note: Read only to point at the alternative; not used or tried in the chapter.

sources.title: Automating Step Functions event delivery with EventBridge
supports: Step Functions sends an Execution Status Change event to EventBridge when the status of a Standard workflow execution changes

sources.title: What is AWS Batch?
supports: AWS Batch plans, schedules, and runs containerized batch jobs on ECS, EKS, Fargate, and EC2 (Spot or On-Demand), provisioning compute in response to submitted jobs

sources.title: AWS Batch: Fargate compute environments
supports: Batch can run jobs on Fargate without managing instances; Fargate is available only for Batch compute environments that use ECS as the orchestrator

sources.title: Cloudflare Workflows
supports: Workflows chain steps with step.do, retry failed steps automatically, and persist state; a WorkflowEntrypoint class defines run(event, step)

sources.title: Cloudflare Workflows: Rules of Workflows
supports: A step might be retried multiple times, so steps should be idempotent
A Workflow may hibernate and lose in-memory state; state must be built from step.do return values, and non-deterministic calls belong inside steps

sources.title: Cloudflare Workflows: Limits
supports: Wall-clock duration per step is unlimited; CPU time per step is 30 seconds by default on the paid plan, configurable to 5 minutes
A step result is at most 1 MiB; a Workflow has at most 10,000 steps by default on the paid plan (1,024 on free)
step.sleep can last up to 365 days
Workers invoked by Cron Triggers and Durable Object alarm handlers have a 15-minute wall time limit

sources.title: Cloudflare Workflows: Pricing
supports: Workflows are billed on CPU time, requests, storage, and steps; a sleeping or waiting Workflow incurs no CPU time
Billing for steps and storage started on 2026-08-10; the paid plan includes 500,000 steps a month

supports: Dedicated providers are registered for AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine, AWS::Scheduler::Schedule, AWS::Lambda::Function, AWS::S3::Bucket, AWS::S3::BucketPolicy, AWS::DynamoDB::Table, AWS::Logs::LogGroup, AWS::IAM::Role, and AWS::IAM::Policy
No provider is registered for AWS::Lambda::Version or AWS::Lambda::Alias, so they go through Cloud Control API
The Step Functions provider applies DefinitionSubstitutions only to a definition fetched from DefinitionS3Location; an inline DefinitionString or Definition is sent as it is
The Lambda function provider passes DurableConfig to CreateFunction and UpdateFunctionConfiguration, and treats adding or removing DurableConfig as a replacement

supports: FunctionProps.durableConfig takes { executionTimeout: Duration; retentionPeriod?: Duration } and renders CfnFunction.DurableConfig
When no role is passed, a function with durableConfig gets the managed policy AWSLambdaBasicDurableExecutionRolePolicy; with a role of your own, nothing is added
CfnStateMachine accepts definitionString, roleArn, and stateMachineType

sources.title: Troubleshoot IAM: Changes that I make are not always immediately visible
supports: IAM uses a distributed computing model called eventual consistency; changes take time to become visible from all possible endpoints
IAM also uses caching, so a change might not be visible until previously cached data times out
AWS recommends not including IAM changes in critical, high-availability code paths, and verifying that changes have propagated before production workflows depend on them

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM
supports: Human users should use federation and temporary credentials; workloads should use IAM roles
Apply least-privilege permissions: grant only the permissions required to perform a task
Get started with AWS managed policies and move toward least-privilege permissions
Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate least-privilege policies based on access activity
Establish permissions guardrails across multiple accounts

sources.title: IAM Access Analyzer policy generation
supports: IAM Access Analyzer reviews CloudTrail logs and generates a policy template containing the permissions an entity used
You specify a time period of up to 90 days, and the CloudTrail trail that is logging events for the account

sources.title: Policy evaluation logic
supports: An explicit deny in any policy overrides an allow
With SCPs, the resulting permissions are the intersection of the identity's policies and the service control policies

sources.title: AWS service reference (secretsmanager, kms, cloudtrail, guardduty, config, organizations, inspector2, iam, cloudformation, logs)
supports: secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, PutSecretValue, and ListSecretVersionIds take the Secret resource type; kms:Decrypt takes the key resource type

The action names used in the SCP exist: organizations:LeaveOrganization, cloudtrail:StopLogging, DeleteTrail, UpdateTrail, PutEventSelectors, guardduty:DeleteDetector, DisassociateFromAdministratorAccount, config:StopConfigurationRecorder, DeleteConfigurationRecorder, DeleteDeliveryChannel

sources.title: Resources that you can protect with AWS WAF
supports: A web ACL can be associated with CloudFront distributions and, regionally, with API Gateway REST APIs, Application Load Balancers, AppSync GraphQL APIs, Cognito user pools, App Runner services, Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Verified Access instances, and Amplify; API Gateway HTTP APIs and Lambda function URLs are not in the list
For CloudFront, the web ACL and everything it uses must be created in US East (N. Virginia)
Each resource can have one web ACL; a web ACL associated with CloudFront distributions cannot be associated with other resource types

sources.title: Using rate-based rule statements in AWS WAF
supports: A rate-based rule costs 2 WCUs as a base
Each use of a rate-based rule is tracked separately

sources.title: Rate-based rule caveats in AWS WAF
supports: AWS WAF applies rate limiting near the limit that you set, but does not guarantee an exact limit match
Requests can come in at too high a rate for up to several minutes before AWS WAF detects and rate limits them; usually the delay is below 30 seconds
Changing a rate limit setting resets the rule's counts and can pause rate limiting for up to a minute

sources.title: Baseline rule groups (AWS Managed Rules)
supports: AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet uses 700 WCUs
Its SizeRestrictions_BODY rule blocks request bodies over 8 KB
For CloudFront the default body inspection limit is 16 KB, and can be raised to 64 KB

sources.title: IP reputation rule groups (AWS Managed Rules)
supports: AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList uses 25 WCUs

sources.title: Web ACL capacity units (WCUs) in AWS WAF
supports: The basic price for a web ACL includes up to 1,500 WCUs; using more incurs additional fees
The maximum capacity for a web ACL is 5,000 WCUs

sources.title: Testing and tuning your AWS WAF protections
supports: AWS recommends testing and tuning rules in count mode with production traffic before enabling them

sources.title: AWS::WAFv2::WebACL
supports: Scope is CLOUDFRONT or REGIONAL; for CLOUDFRONT the resource must be created in us-east-1
DefaultAction, Scope, and VisibilityConfig are required

sources.title: AWS::WAFv2::WebACL RateBasedStatement
supports: Limit has a minimum of 10
EvaluationWindowSec may be 60, 120, 300, or 600, and defaults to 300
AWS WAF checks the rate about every 10 seconds

sources.title: Use AWS WAF protections (CloudFront)
supports: AWS WAF can be enabled on a distribution with one-click protection in the CloudFront console or with a preconfigured web ACL

sources.title: Restrict access to an AWS Lambda function URL origin
supports: With origin access control, PUT and POST requests need the SHA-256 of the body in the x-amz-content-sha256 header, supplied by the caller
CloudFront signs an origin request by adding its own Authorization header; the no-override setting passes the viewer's Authorization header through instead

sources.title: AWS Price List: AWS WAF
supports: Global-WebACLV2: USD 5.00 per web ACL per month, prorated hourly
Global-RuleV2: USD 1.00 per rule per month, prorated hourly
Global-RequestV2-Tier1: USD 0.60 per million requests
The same three prices appear under the ap-northeast-1 and us-east-1 usage types

sources.title: What's in a Secrets Manager secret?
supports: A secret has versions; Secrets Manager tracks three by staging label: AWSCURRENT, AWSPREVIOUS, and AWSPENDING
A secret always has a version labeled AWSCURRENT, and that version is returned by default
Unlabeled versions are deprecated and removed when there are more than 100; versions created less than 24 hours ago are not removed
The secret ARN ends in six random characters, so a secret re-created under the same name has a different ARN

sources.title: PutSecretValue
supports: Without VersionStages, AWSCURRENT moves to the new version and AWSPREVIOUS moves to the version AWSCURRENT was removed from
The operation is idempotent: the same ClientRequestToken with the same secret data succeeds and does nothing; with different data it fails
ClientRequestToken becomes the VersionId of the new version
Do not call PutSecretValue at a sustained rate of more than once every 10 minutes

sources.title: GetSecretValue
supports: VersionStage selects a version by staging label; without it AWSCURRENT is returned
AWS recommends caching secret values on the client to improve speed and reduce cost
With a customer managed key the caller also needs kms:Decrypt on that key

sources.title: DeleteSecret
supports: A deleted secret has a recovery window: minimum 7 days, default 30 days
While scheduled for deletion, the secret value cannot be retrieved

sources.title: AWS Secrets Manager best practices
supports: The supported caching components are for Java, Python, .NET, Go, and Rust, plus the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension; none is listed for JavaScript

sources.title: Rotation by Lambda function
supports: A rotation function has four steps: createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, finishSecret
Secrets Manager uses staging labels to identify versions during rotation

sources.title: AWS Secrets Manager pricing
supports: Secrets are billed per secret per month, prorated by the hour for secrets stored less than a month
A replica secret is billed as a distinct secret

sources.title: AWS Price List: AWS Secrets Manager (ap-northeast-1)
supports: USD 0.40 per secret per month
USD 0.05 per 10,000 API requests

sources.title: AWS::SecretsManager::Secret
supports: GenerateSecretString generates the value; SecretString sets a specific one
Without KmsKeyId, Secrets Manager uses the key aws/secretsmanager

sources.title: Working with Lambda environment variables
supports: AWS recommends Secrets Manager instead of environment variables for database credentials, API keys, and authorization tokens

sources.title: Use Secrets Manager secrets in Lambda functions
supports: AWS describes two ready-made approaches: the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension and the Powertools for AWS Lambda parameters utility; both keep a local cache
The extension caches secrets for 300 seconds by default

sources.title: AWS KMS keys
supports: Customer managed keys carry a monthly fee and a per-use fee; AWS managed keys carry no monthly fee
AWS managed keys are created, managed, and used on your behalf by an AWS service; they rotate every year
Unless you are required to control the key, an AWS managed key is a good choice

sources.title: Rotate AWS KMS keys
supports: With automatic rotation enabled, AWS KMS generates new key material every year by default
AWS KMS charges a monthly fee for the first and second rotation of key material; the increase is capped at the second rotation

sources.title: Delete an AWS KMS key
supports: Deleting a KMS key requires a waiting period of 7 to 30 days; the default is 30
A key pending deletion cannot be used in any cryptographic operation
Deletion can be cancelled before the waiting period ends, and not after

sources.title: AWS KMS pricing
supports: Each KMS key you create costs USD 1 a month, prorated hourly
The first and second rotation of a key each add USD 1 a month
AWS KMS provides a free tier of 20,000 requests a month, calculated across all Regions
There is no charge for creating and storing AWS managed keys

sources.title: AWS Price List: AWS KMS (ap-northeast-1)
supports: USD 1 per customer managed KMS key version per month
USD 0.03 per 10,000 requests
A Global-KMS-Requests SKU at USD 0 covers the first 20,000 requests a month

sources.title: What is Amazon GuardDuty?
supports: GuardDuty is a threat detection service that monitors and analyzes AWS data sources and logs
It detects, for example, compromised credentials, cryptomining, and unusual login patterns
Foundational threat detection starts ingesting CloudTrail events, VPC flow logs, and DNS logs when GuardDuty is enabled

sources.title: Getting started with GuardDuty
supports: Enabling GuardDuty for the first time in a Region also enables, by default, all protection types available in that Region
AWS recommends enabling GuardDuty in all supported Regions

sources.title: Monitoring GuardDuty usage and estimating costs
supports: GuardDuty offers a 30-day free trial per account for most protection plans
Usage and estimated cost can be monitored in the GuardDuty console

sources.title: AWS Price List: Amazon GuardDuty (ap-northeast-1)

sources.title: What is Amazon Inspector?
supports: Inspector is a vulnerability management service that scans workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure
It scans EC2 instances, container images in ECR, and Lambda functions

sources.title: Scanning AWS Lambda functions with Amazon Inspector
supports: Lambda standard scanning checks application dependencies for package vulnerabilities; code scanning is a separate, optional type
On activation Inspector scans functions invoked or updated in the last 90 days, and rescans on deploys and when a new CVE is added
Inspector does not scan Lambda functions encrypted with customer managed keys

sources.title: Getting started with Amazon Inspector
supports: Activating Inspector for a standalone account in the console activates all scan types by default

sources.title: Amazon Inspector pricing
supports: Accounts new to Inspector get a 15-day free trial
Lambda standard scanning is billed per function, prorated by coverage hours

sources.title: AWS Price List: Amazon Inspector (ap-northeast-1)
supports: Lambda standard scanning: USD 0.0005 per function-hour

sources.title: Working with CloudTrail event history
supports: CloudTrail is enabled by default; event history holds the past 90 days of management events in a Region
Event history is immutable, and there is no CloudTrail charge for viewing it

sources.title: CloudTrail concepts
supports: Events created by CloudFront, IAM, and AWS STS are recorded in us-east-1
Event history and lookup-events show global service events in the Region where they occurred

sources.title: LookupEvents
supports: Looks up management events from the last 90 days in a Region
At most 50 results per call; lookup requests are limited to two per second per account per Region

sources.title: AWS CloudTrail pricing
supports: The 90-day event history is available at no additional cost
One copy of ongoing management events can be delivered to S3 for free by creating a trail; additional copies cost USD 2.00 per 100,000 events

sources.title: What is AWS Config?
supports: AWS Config records the configuration of resources and how configurations and relationships change over time

sources.title: AWS Config pricing
supports: You pay per configuration item delivered, per account per Region
Recording can be continuous or periodic (once every 24 hours, only if a change occurred)

sources.title: AWS Price List: AWS Config (ap-northeast-1)
supports: USD 0.003 per configuration item recorded continuously
USD 0.012 per configuration item recorded daily

sources.title: Service control policies (SCPs)
supports: SCPs do not grant permissions; they set the maximum available permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts
SCPs need an organization with all features enabled
SCPs do not affect users or roles in the management account, or service-linked roles
AWS strongly recommends not attaching SCPs to the root without testing; removing FullAWSAccess without a replacement makes all actions fail

sources.title: SCP evaluation
supports: An action needs an explicit Allow at every level from the root through each OU to the account
A Deny at any level denies the action for everything beneath it
Organizations attaches the AWS managed SCP FullAWSAccess when SCPs are enabled

sources.title: SCP syntax
supports: Principal and NotPrincipal are not supported in SCPs
Action, NotAction, Resource, NotResource, and Condition are supported in Allow and Deny statements
The example that denies operations outside chosen Regions uses NotAction with cloudfront:*, iam:*, route53:*, support:* and StringNotEquals on aws:RequestedRegion

sources.title: Quotas and service limits for AWS Organizations
supports: The maximum size of a service control policy document is 10,240 characters

sources.title: Create an organization with AWS Organizations
supports: The account that creates an organization becomes its management account
An organization supports all features by default, or consolidated billing only

sources.title: AWS Organizations FAQs
supports: AWS Organizations is offered at no additional charge

supports: The root-user example denies with ArnLike on aws:PrincipalArn arn:aws:iam::*:root

sources.title: Point-in-time backups for DynamoDB
supports: Point-in-time recovery gives continuous backups with up to 35 days of recovery points at per-second granularity

sources.title: Enable point-in-time recovery in DynamoDB
supports: PITR is charged on the size of the table, including local secondary indexes, until it is turned off; the recovery period does not affect the price
A restore is possible to any point between EarliestRestorableDateTime and LatestRestorableDateTime, and LatestRestorableDateTime is typically five minutes before the current time
The point-in-time recovery process always restores to a new table
ContinuousBackupsStatus is always ENABLED; whether a table can be restored is PointInTimeRecoveryStatus, which is DISABLED by default
Deleting a table that has PITR enabled creates a system backup that is kept for 35 days at no additional cost

sources.title: Restoring a DynamoDB table to a point in time
supports: The source table stays available for reads and writes while the restore runs

While a restore is in progress the table shows as being created with restore in progress, and becomes ACTIVE when it is finished

sources.title: How DynamoDB global tables work
supports: In the default consistency mode, item changes are replicated asynchronously to all other replicas, typically within a second or less
Conflicting writes are resolved by last writer wins

sources.title: Working with delete markers
supports: A DELETE without a version ID in a versioning-enabled bucket does not delete the object: a delete marker becomes the current version
A GET without a version ID on a key whose current version is a delete marker returns 404
Delete markers are listed only by ListObjectVersions; ListObjectsV2 does not return keys whose current version is a delete marker
A delete marker is billed for the size of its key name

sources.title: Managing delete markers
supports: To undelete an object, delete its delete marker with a DeleteObject request that names the marker's version ID
A DeleteObject without a version ID on a key whose current version is a delete marker removes nothing and adds another delete marker
An expired object delete marker is one with no versions left under it, and a lifecycle rule can remove it

sources.title: Restoring previous versions
supports: A previous version is restored either by copying it into the same bucket, which makes the copy the current version and preserves all versions, or by permanently deleting the current version

sources.title: ListObjectVersions

sources.title: Lifecycle configuration elements
supports: NoncurrentVersionExpiration permanently deletes noncurrent versions a number of days after they became noncurrent; they cannot be recovered

ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker removes delete markers that have no versions left

sources.title: What does Amazon S3 replicate?

sources.title: Replicating delete markers between buckets

sources.title: celld v0.6.2: README
supports: celld runs a Cloudflare Workers application on your own machines and stores long-term state in an S3-compatible, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage bucket
A node is one celld process; nodes that share one bucket are a fleet; a conditional bucket write gives a node the ownership of a cell
celld uses the standard AWS credential chain; a node is started with --bucket, --listen, --internal-listen, and --advertise
The container example sets CELLD_WATCH to a directory on a persistent volume
One node proves each write through the bucket; with a second node the write finishes once that node holds it on disk
Put every advertised address on a trusted private network or an encrypted overlay; celld rejects a literal public IP unless --unsafe-public-advertise is given
Treat access to the bucket and its credentials as fleet administrator access
The installer downloads the binary from GitHub releases; provenance is verifiable with gh attestation verify

sources.title: celld v0.6.2: documentation (operate, shut down, upgrade notes, environment variables)
supports: CELLD_DURABILITY defaults to fleet; a one-node fleet waits for the bucket on every write; a fleet that loses all but one node falls back to the bucket and stays correct

celld shuts down gracefully on SIGTERM or SIGINT: health reports 503, accepted requests finish, and the node hands its cells off to a peer; POST /shutdown on the internal listener starts the same handoff
CELLD_SHUTDOWN_TOTAL_MS defaults to 40000; the orchestrator stop grace (systemd TimeoutStopSec) must be above it or SIGKILL can interrupt the handoff
To roll out a new version: stop each node with SIGTERM, wait for its replacement to report healthy, then move to the next node
During a rolling update, wait for restoring=0 on every node (celld diagnose) before restarting the next
A new process does not report healthy until the fleet settles; CELLD_READY_FLEET_GATE_MS defaults to 120000

Upgrade notes: v0.1.0 to v0.2.0 stop all; v0.2.1 to v0.3.0 rolling; v0.3.0 to v0.4.0 stop all; v0.4.0 to v0.4.1 rolling; v0.5.1 to v0.6.0 stop all with fleet durability; v0.6.0 to v0.6.1 rolling; v0.6.1 to v0.6.2 rolling

The node lease lives CELLD_TTL_MS (default 10000) and renews at one third of that; the fleet sample is read every CELLD_REBALANCE_INTERVAL_MS (default 5000); deploy/current.json is read every CELLD_DEPLOY_POLL_S (default 30)
CELLD_BUCKET, AWS_REGION, CELLD_ADDR, CELLD_INTERNAL_ADDR, CELLD_ADVERTISE, and CELLD_WATCH are the environment forms of the node settings; CELLD_NODE is an explicit node-session ID
A bucket value can add a key prefix (s3://BUCKET/PREFIX)
celld deploy needs esbuild on PATH for Worker code; CELLD_ESBUILD overrides the path; a running node adopts a new deployment without a restart
celld diagnose reads the node leases and probes each live peer without taking a lease; celld cell list prints one Class:ID scope per line
One 8 GB node holds 1,000 resident cells
celld does not scale itself; an external system starts and stops the nodes

sources.title: celld v0.6.2: what celld guarantees
supports: Two promises: exactly one node serves a cell at a time, and an acknowledged write is never lost; both require a bucket with working conditional writes and ranged reads, and a supervisor that restarts the process
The qualified stores are Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Tigris, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage; the release tests run against R2, and the S3 path uses the same client and headers
The supervisor must restart without an attempt limit and wait at least one lease lifetime between attempts
Each cell has one ownership record in the bucket, naming the owner's session and a fencing epoch, acquired by conditional create or compare-and-swap

In fleet mode the owner sends each write to one or two followers and every follower must fsync it; a fleet needs two running nodes for a fleet proof; a fleet of three or more holds three copies of an acknowledged write
In fleet mode celld can acknowledge a write before its bucket upload completes; a follower disk can hold acknowledged writes that the bucket does not yet hold
Recovery limits: a follower's HTTP error can block recovery and startup; a deleted final batch is undetectable if nothing later records its range; a mixed-version tail can stall recovery
A node whose lease expires fences itself, logs a line starting with SELF-FENCE:, and exits with code 3; only a restart returns it
celld reserves the key prefixes probe/, cells/, nodes/, node-cells/, fleet/, deploy/, deploy-blobs/, log/, wake/, and telemetry/

The v0.4.1 upgrade procedure: stop every node and wait for every lease to expire, back up the bucket and node data keeping node names, peer addresses, and data directories; to roll back, restore the full stopped-fleet backup, which loses writes made after it
Each node runs the storage test (four conditional writes and a ranged read) before it serves, and cannot disable it

sources.title: celld v0.6.2: testing
supports: The coordination protocol is specified in TLA+ and exercised by deterministic simulation; the model grants a linearizable object store
Live-fleet fault scenarios include SIGKILL mid-write-stream, freezing an owner, cutting a node off from the bucket, and stopping a host; a verification pass fetches each cell through different nodes
A cell can be briefly unavailable while ownership moves
A fleet at its resident limit has no space for a lost node's cells
